what: Ameris Bancorp is a bank in the American Southeast. It takes deposits and lends across Georgia, Florida, Alabama, South Carolina and North Carolina, with a substantial national mortgage origination business alongside commercial and commercial real estate lending.
customers: Small and mid-sized businesses, commercial property developers, and homebuyers nationally through its mortgage division, plus retail depositors across the Southeast.
money: The spread between interest earned on loans and paid on deposits.
Mortgage origination and sale, plus service charges and other fee income.
moat: A deposit franchise in fast-growing southeastern markets is a valuable asset: population and business formation in Georgia, Florida and the Carolinas run well ahead of the national average, which supplies loan demand and deposit growth without taking share from anyone. Local lending relationships built over decades are the other durable advantage.
risks: Commercial real estate is the sector’s main concern and is a meaningful share of the loan book.
The mortgage business makes earnings more volatile than a pure commercial bank’s, because origination volumes swing with interest rates.
Revenue growth has been modest, from $1.1B in 2022 to $1.2B in 2025.
Interest rates set by the Federal Reserve determine the net interest margin, not management.
Only six analysts cover the stock, so the $93.17 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: A trailing net margin of about 34% and free cash flow of $635.2M on $1.3B of revenue.
The shares trade at about 14.1 times earnings, 8.3 times EV/EBITDA and 8.5 times free cash flow.
Cash of $1.1B against only $50.7M of holding company debt is a conservative structure.
Southeastern markets are among the fastest growing in the United States for population and business formation.
Mortgage origination becomes a significant earnings contributor when rates fall, which gives some natural hedge.
watch: Non-performing loans and the composition of the commercial real estate book. In banking, credit is the only thing that turns a good year into a disaster.
view: Geography matters more in banking than almost anywhere else, and Ameris has the better geography. Georgia, Florida and the Carolinas are among the fastest-growing states in America for both population and business formation, which means a bank there gets loan demand and deposit growth without having to take share from competitors. That is a structurally easier position than a bank in a flat or declining region, and it is worth a premium.

The composition of the business is less straightforward. Alongside conventional commercial banking sits a substantial national mortgage origination operation, which makes earnings considerably more volatile than a pure commercial bank’s. Mortgage origination collapses when rates rise and surges when they fall, so a quarter’s results can swing for reasons that have nothing to do with the lending franchise. That cuts both ways — it is a natural hedge against falling rates compressing the net interest margin — but it makes the earnings harder to read.

The balance sheet is conservative where it should be: $1.1 billion of cash against only $51 million of holding company debt. A bank’s holding company borrowing is the thing that turns a credit problem into a solvency problem, and there is very little of it here. That matters more than it sounds going into a period where commercial real estate losses are still emerging.

And those losses are the open question, as they are for every regional bank. Commercial real estate defaults slowly, because a loan does not fail until it matures and cannot be refinanced at today’s rates — so the picture takes two or three more years of maturities to clarify, and a bank that looks fine now can look different afterwards. At 14.1 times earnings, Ameris is priced at a modest premium to peers, which the growth footprint arguably justifies. Non-performing loans, and what sits inside the commercial real estate book, are the figures that decide whether the premium survives.
bull: Fast-growing southeastern markets supply loan and deposit growth, a conservative holding company absorbs any credit stress, and mortgage income surges if rates fall.
bear: Commercial real estate losses emerge as loans mature, mortgage volatility obscures the deterioration, and a premium multiple contracts to the sector average.
